headline: Ressha is from Sinitic 列車 (lièchē).
Shūkyō is 宗 (shū, “doctrine”) plus 教 (kyō, “teaching”), repurposed near the start of the Meiji period to translate English religion.
Kōchō is 校 (kō, “school”) plus 長 (chō, “chief”).
Kokoroeru is from the classical verb kokorou, written 心得.
Keiyōdōshi is 形容 (keiyō, “description; form”) plus 動詞 (dōshi, “verb”).
Gomen nasai is the honorific imperative of 免ずる (menzuru, “to spare; to exempt”).
Kenkyū's first character 研 originally read gen; for reasons unknown the reading shifted to a kan'yō yomi of ken.
Yūmoa is a transliteration of English humour or humor.
Fumikiri is fumi, the stem of 踏む (fumu, “step on”), plus kiri, the stem of 切る (kiru).
Yōhinten is 洋品 (yōhin) plus 店 (-ten).
Nōka is from Sinitic 農家 (nóngjiā).
Kusuri appears to be the stem of an unattested verb kusuru, “to have a mystical effect”.
Saku, “to bloom”, is simply from Old Japanese.
Nō, “brain”, is from Middle Chinese 腦, and went from nau through nɔː to noː.
Erebētā is borrowed from American English elevator.
Ippai, “full”, is literally 一 (ichi, “one”) plus 杯 (hai, “cupful”).
Hige has several theories, including hohoge (頬 “cheek” plus 毛 “hair”) and hirakuke (開く “to open” plus 毛), literally “hair of the opening”.
Fukamaru is 深 (fuka) plus まる (-maru, “to become (an adjective), -en”).
Irassharu was originally a contraction of いらせらる (iraseraru), an honorific conjugation of the verb iru.
Machiaishitsu is machiai, the stem of 待ち合う (machiau), plus 室 (-shitsu, “room”).
Maku, “curtain”, is from Middle Chinese 幕 (MC mak).
Naze began as nani semu ni, from Old Japanese 何せむに.
De wa is a clipping of ではないか (de wa nai ka, “isn't it; might it be”).
Mujun is literally 矛 (“lance, spear”) plus 盾 (“shield”).
Kōtsū is Middle Chinese 交通, literally “cross through”.
Kanji is the continuative stem of the verbs 感ずる (kanzuru) and 感じる (kanjiru, “to feel”).
Denryoku is 電 (den, “electric”) plus 力 (-ryoku, “power”).
Hoeru is from Proto-Japonic *pəyu, and cognate with Kunigami buirun.
Dō is first cited to 1604 in the Portuguese work Arte da Lingoa de Iapam.
Shinzō is 心 (shin, “heart”) plus 臓 (zō, “internal organ”).
Kakuchō is 拡 (kaku, “expand”) plus 張 (chō, “stretch”).
